slides.0.title: From colonial vineyards to foreign-funded revival
slides.0.subtitle: Morocco's wine fortunes were set mainly by markets and policy
slides.1.title: The French era: planted for export
slides.1.highlights.0.title: Ancient beginnings
slides.1.highlights.0.content: Phoenicians are generally believed to have brought vine-growing, and it was established under Rome. Details are thin, so a general awareness is enough
slides.1.highlights.1.title: Large-scale planting
slides.1.highlights.1.content: Vineyards on a large scale came with French colonists, much as in Algeria
slides.1.highlights.2.title: The 1950s peak
slides.1.highlights.2.content: At independence in 1956 there were roughly 55,000–70,000 ha producing 2–3 million hl a year. Sources differ, so remember the scale rather than one figure
slides.1.content: The main outlet for this wine was France, so trouble came quickly after independence.
slides.2.title: After independence: lost markets, ageing vines
slides.2.highlights.0.title: The 1967 quotas
slides.2.highlights.0.content: The European Economic Community introduced import quotas in 1967, sharply reducing the export market
slides.2.highlights.1.title: State control
slides.2.highlights.1.content: From the 1970s the state took over most vineyards, and the state agricultural company SODEA dates from this period. Fixed grape prices gave no incentive for quality
slides.2.highlights.2.title: The low point in the early 1990s
slides.2.highlights.2.content: The Oxford Companion to Wine records about 13,000 ha for wine at the time, over half of it old or diseased
slides.2.content: From peak to low point took under forty years, and the causes were lost markets and missing incentives, not terroir.
slides.3.title: The 1990s: leasing land to foreign firms
slides.3.highlights.0.title: Long leases
slides.3.highlights.0.content: Under Hassan II foreign firms could take long leases on state vineyards from SODEA. French money followed, with Groupe Castel the leading example
slides.3.highlights.1.title: Replanting
slides.3.highlights.1.content: Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot and Syrah began to grow quickly, reaching about 15% together by 2005
slides.3.highlights.2.title: A higher tier
slides.3.highlights.2.content: AOGs date from 1977. In 1998 general rules for AOCs were issued along with the first AOC, Les Coteaux de l'Atlas
slides.3.content: Today's Moroccan wine is the product of that wave of foreign capital and replanting.
slides.4.componentProps.slide.title: 🧠 Knowledge check
Morocco's vineyards expanded on a large scale under the French. When did it gain independence?
1912 is the start of the protectorate; 1977 and 1998 are the AOG and AOC rules.
What badly hit Moroccan wine exports in 1967?
A. A total ban on alcohol
The lost market started the decline; state control came later.
What was the key to the 1990s revival?
A. Replanting everything to native grapes
B. Banning domestic sales and exporting everything
C. Co-operatives buying all the vineyards
D. Foreign firms leasing state vineyards long-term from SODEA
This brought in French capital such as Castel, along with replanting.
